extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing, judging, and anticipating reception of poetry and literary works; includes stylistic rules (diction, epithets, imagery), critical maxims, and practical advice about publication and audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for admission of double epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for the admission of double epithets seems to be this: either that they should be already denizens of our language, such as blood-stained, terror-stricken, self-applauding: or when a new epithet, or one found in books only, is hazarded, that it, at least, be one word, not two words made one by mere virtue of the printers hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: Compare Milton’s early poems (many double epithets) with Paradise Lost (few) and Paradise Regained (scarce). If you must risk a novel epithet, prefer a single-word formation rather than a two-word hyphenated construct. The English language (being almost without cases) is unfitted for loose compounds; seek alternate expression where possible. (Cf. examples: blood-stained, terror-stricken vs. avoid awkward hyphenations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid words translatable into simpler equivalent phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is translatable in other and simpler words of the same language, without loss of sense or dignity, is bad. N.B.--By dignity I mean the absence of ludicrous and debasing associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a regula maxima of criticism: if a phrase can be rendered more simply without loss, the more complex phrasing is a fault. The note emphasizes preserving 'dignity'—avoid simpler substitutions that introduce ludicrous or debasing associations. Use this as a test for overwrought diction and needless ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or awkward compounds; prefer alternate expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A language which, like the English, is almost without cases, is indeed in its very genius unfitted for compounds. If a writer, every time a compounded word suggests itself to him, would seek for some other mode of expressing the same sense, the chances are always greatly in favour of his finding a better word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: when tempted by a compounded or novel coined word, try to express the idea differently—often a better, clearer word exists. Caesar’s maxim (Ut tanquam scopulum sic fugias insolens verbum) is invoked: avoid 'insolens' or odd words. Examples in the notes contrast successful single-word compounds with awkward new formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from canonical models (Milton, Shakespeare, Pope, Spenser, Fletcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of Milton and Shakespeare may be usefully pointed out to young authors... The rule for the admission of double epithets seems to be this... I had derived peculiar advantages from my school discipline, and though my general theory of poetry was the same then as now, I had yet experienced the same sensations myself, and felt almost as if I had been newly couched, when, by Mr. Wordsworth’s conversation, I had been induced to re-examine with impartial strictness Gray’s celebrated Elegy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: study great predecessors to observe how they handle devices (epithets, compounds, diction, blank verse harmony). Use their restraint and strengths as instructive examples rather than imitation of superficial features. The text repeatedly recommends comparing early and late works of master poets to see how stylistic choices change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for performance/recitation effects on reception
rubrics_metrics.description: In their calculations on the probable reception of a poem, they must subtract to a large amount from the panegyric, which may have encouraged them to publish it... the excitement and temporary sympathy of feeling, which the recitation of the poem by an admirer, especially if he be at once a warm admirer and a man of acknowledged celebrity, calls forth in the audience... This is really a species of animal magnetism, in which the enkindling reciter, by perpetual comment of looks and tones, lends his own will and apprehensive faculty to his auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting or evaluating a poem’s success, adjust for the boost given by enthusiastic public recitation or celebrated advocates. Recitation can create temporary sympathy that inflates apparent merit; a poem 'left to itself' may not produce the same effect. Practically: do not equate recitation-induced applause with intrinsic textual quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtract non-literary factors when estimating critical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowances must be made for private enmity... for personal enmity behind the mask of anonymous criticism: secondly for the necessity of a certain proportion of abuse and ridicule in a Review, in order to make it saleable... but lastly and chiefly, for the excitement and temporary sympathy of feeling ... called forth in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: factors skewing reception include private or anonymous hostility, commercial incentives of reviewers to include abuse/ridicule, lack of influential friends behind the scenes, and recitation effects. Authors and critics should consider these when judging reviews or the impact of publication; adjust interpretations of praise and blame accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules are means to ends; ascertain the end before prescribing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics are too apt to forget, that rules are but means to an end; consequently, where the ends are different, the rules must be likewise so. We must have ascertained what the end is, before we can determine what the rules ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or applying critical rules for drama, poetry, or other forms, first determine the intended purpose or 'end' of the work. Do not rigidly apply inherited rules from another historical or cultural context (e.g., Greek stage rules) without assessing whether those rules serve the work’s aims. This is a caution against mechanical formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer collective meaning and sense over isolated admired phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: The impression on the audience in general was sudden and evident: and a number of enlightened and highly educated persons... acknowledged--(so much had they been accustomed, in reading poetry, to receive pleasure from the separate images and phrases successively, without asking themselves whether the collective meaning was sense or nonsense)--that they might in all probability have read the same passage again twenty times with undiminished admiration, and without once reflecting...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: beware of being won by individual poetic images or phrases while ignoring whether they fit together into coherent sense. Critique and editing should assess the overall semantic integrity of a passage, not just the brilliance of isolated lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve consistency and appropriateness in imagery and similes (avoid bombast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more simple as a description, or more accurate as a simile; which, (says Seward,) is thus finely translated by Mr. Pope... Now here--(not to mention the tremendous bombast)--the Dog Star, so called, is turned into a real dog, a very odd dog, a fire, fever, plague, and death-breathing, red, air-tainting dog: and the whole visual likeness is lost, while the likeness in the effects is rendered absurd by the exaggeration. In Spenser and Fletcher the thought is justifiable; for the images are at least consistent, and it was the intention of the writers to mark the seasons by this allegory of visualized puns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing similes, ensure the visual likeness and the effects align coherently; avoid exaggeration that destroys the original likeness or produces absurdity. The example contrasts Spenser/Fletcher (consistent images) with a bombastic translation that turns a star into an incoherent monstrous dog—an anti-pattern to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware pseudo-poetic diction produced by imitative translations
rubrics_metrics.description: I had occasion to point out the almost faultless position and choice of words, in Pope’s original compositions, particularly in his Satires and moral Essays, for the purpose of comparing them with his translation of Homer, which, I do not stand alone in regarding, as the main source of our pseudo-poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: translations and influential earlier works can create fashions of 'pseudo-poetic' diction that corrupt taste; authors should be cautious about adopting such diction uncritically. Analyze whether admired stylistic traits (often learned from translations) contribute to sense and integrity, not just surface ornament.
